[messages6.html|6 June 2026] before focusing on the front end, let's make sure the ourcome proces from watson are enterprise grade, bellingcat grate, Watson-grade (e.g. good enough to be publshed ad .md to make the intelligence brain more an more poweful over time, and compete with Palantir). principle of data collection of bellingcat: Bellingcat regularly uses material shared online by individuals from a wide variety of locations and backgrounds. This is only natural given our focus on open source data and investigations. Despite the material being publicly available, however, Bellingcat considers the following questions when it uses the information it has gathered: 
Does using the information serve an investigative purpose and is it in the public interest? If so, to what extent? The information must at least serve both of these purposes to be used and published as part of our investigations. 
Could anybody be harmed by publishing the information? If so, to what extent? Do any elements of the information pose risks to a person’s private life? What is the potential impact if information is erroneous or out of date? Are victims appropriately protected from those consequences? 
Are there alternative approaches that would maximise the public purpose, such as combining material we may have found with information from other databases? Are there alternatives that would minimise harm? 
Can the data be verified? Have reasonable steps been taken to verify the accuracy of the information? Can people in the investigation be notified before publication? What can be done to enable correction of errors identified after publication? 
The ethical issues raised by the use of open source information are at the forefront of any decision to use data. As we often deal with issues related to rights violations and crimes, we must ensure that the identities of victims are protected and that those not directly involved in the violations are not exposed to harassment or other negative consequences as a result of our publications. Those documenting war crimes are particularly vulnerable given they often share images from active conflict zones, where local authorities can target them for retaliation. For example, it may be possible to geolocate a video to a specific location. But if the video is filmed from the home of a human rights activist, publishing that information can lead authorities to the door of that very activist. 
We also consider the status of an individual and the civic value in publishing information about them. Children are particularly vulnerable, and when relevant images are used that contain images of children we take steps to remove the children from the images. We also do not use images unless they are relevant to our stories and refrain from publishing images for shock value or to scandalise private individuals. 
Datasets collected by Bellingcat are only shared externally with other organisations where the intent is to build on the original purpose of the data collection, or where there is a new purpose that meets the goals and objectives of Bellingcat. For example, our dataset of videos showing violence against journalists at Black Lives Matter protests was initially used for Bellingcat’s own reporting on the violence, it was later shared with the Global Legal Action Network to build a legal case for challenging the use of riot equipment and non-lethal arms exports to the US from the UK. When working with other organisations to build datasets, agreements are first reached on how those data will be used in line with Bellingcat’s data policy, goals and objectives. Datasets are not to be used for commercial purposes nor sold to third parties. editorial practices and standards: Who We Are and What We Do 
Bellingcat is an independent collective of researchers, investigators and citizen journalists who specialise in open source and social media investigation.

---

[messages6.html|6 June 2026] Our field is an exciting one and sees a variety of disciplines, such as advanced technology, forensic research and journalism come together. With the convergence of so many diverse fields and skill sets, forging a unique set of editorial guidelines by which to operate is a challenge. 
Yet doing so is vitally important to ensure trust in the work we do. What follows is an overview of the standards and practices that we at Bellingcat will look to hold ourselves to. These should also act as a guide to our researchers, editors and contributors. 
Needless to say, what is written here will evolve as time passes and new challenges arise. No matter where our work takes us, we will always seek to apply the highest professional and ethical principles to what we do. 
Values 
We aim to achieve fairness and accuracy in our work at all times. We regularly report on issues of justice, transparency and accountability. As such, it is only fair that we look to hold our own work to these values. 
We seek to establish facts through objectively documented evidence, presented completely and in full context. Our researchers seek to report fairly, transparently and without bias, fear or favour. 
Impartiality 
Bellingcat is editorially independent. 
While we commit to investigate wrongdoing wherever it may occur, the strictest standards of fairness and impartiality must be applied at all times. 
From time to time, Bellingcat may look to partner with other organisations. However, if the behaviour or standards of any prospective partner falls below that expected by Bellingcat, we will not work with them. 
Journalistic and Research Ethics 
When individuals or organisations are accused of wrongdoing, we will seek to give them the right to reply and a reasonable amount of time to respond. 
Accusations will only be made when there is a sound, evidential basis for doing so. Given the nature of some Bellingcat reports, however, we recognise some people may not be contactable (be they spies, drug lords, terrorists, or anyone who makes a point of being hard to find; also persons or organisations who have stated they will not honour right of reply approaches from Bellingcat). 
Our researchers will always consider the potential consequences of publication for vulnerable groups or individuals. In certain circumstances, this may require us to balance such concerns with the wider public interest and vice versa. 
Our researchers do not steal information and do not pay individuals or witnesses for their statements. We commit to practising good journalistic and research principles at all times. 
Transparency 
We aim to promote the use of open source tools for investigation and we encourage others to try these methods for themselves. 
However, we want people to do so openly and responsibly. We commit to lead the way by operating to the highest standards in this regard. Our researchers will be as clear as possible with potential sources and subjects as to who they are, who they work for and what their intentions are when undertaking research. 
There may be occasions when researchers have to disguise their online identity in order to expose wrongdoing. However, this course of action must not be taken lightly. Such investigations must be targeted, in the wider public interest and not done frivolously. In such circumstances, our researchers must not seek to needlessly draw in or interact with people who are not targets of their investigation. 
We will always seek to be open about the methods and tools we use as well as the sources of our information.

---

[messages6.html|6 June 2026] Given our commitment to transparency, the use of anonymous sources is generally avoided. However, there may be isolated occasions when this is acceptable. Researchers should discuss any such instances where they believe an exception may apply with senior staff. All information from anonymous sources will be rigorously checked against open source evidence and other data. For the avoidance of doubt, information from an anonymous source should only be used as an intelligence lead and must be validated by objective, open-source and/or reproducible methods that would permit other media organisations or researchers to independently validate such facts. 
Commitment to Accuracy 
When our researchers and contributors submit stories, they go through a process of fact-checking and review by their fellow researchers before editing. However, information should be checked and double-checked by the authors of articles before they are submitted for review. 
Researchers are expected to be fair, accurate and clearly show their work. Editors and reviewers will raise any questions they have before publication. If articles do not reach Bellingcat’s standards, as described here, they will not be published. 
We accept pitches from outside contributors, all of whom are expected to operate to the same standards as our researchers. 
Plagiarism 
Plagiarism is never acceptable and will be dealt with severely. We strive to be original in all the work we do. 
Privacy and Harm 
Researchers must not go beyond what is reasonably required to obtain evidence of suspected wrongdoing. 
They must not harass individuals they may be reporting on. It is important researchers act proportionately at all times when investigating and seeking comment from people who may form part of the stories they are working on. 
Researchers must exercise caution when dealing with information they find during investigations and not publish private details without fully justifiable public interest reasons. Care must also be taken to not unnecessarily reveal information or images of those who may be family members or related to the subjects of our investigations. Bellingcat encourages other media who may build upon our work to follow these principles as well. 
When justified, we may place notices on our stories emphasising these points. When using content from social media, due concern should be given to individuals who appear or may be identifiable in the images or video. This is especially the case if they did not create or post the content in question. Researchers must also consider the consequences for vulnerable groups who may be identifiable in videos or images before using such content in articles and investigations. 
The impact on victims, survivors or relatives who have suffered loss due to accidents, or disasters must also be carefully considered. If researchers have to approach them during the course of their work, they must act with compassion and understanding. Researchers must also consider the consequences of publishing details in stories that may add to any suffering or loss sustained by such individuals. 
Clarification and Corrections 
If it becomes apparent that information in our articles is incorrect, we will seek to clarify and amend as soon as possible. 
Any corrections will be clearly noted at the bottom of articles where incorrect information appeared. 
Misspellings, typos and errors of grammar do not require a factual correction unless they relate to the likes of a name or a place. 
Researchers should report anything that needs correcting to editors and senior staff. 
Copyright and Images 
We commit to using images and comments in context and never in a manner that may be misleading. All images must be clearly credited and described accurately. Anyone unsure about the rights to use particular images should ask editors.

---

[messages6.html|6 June 2026] In some cases it may be preferential to use screenshots instead of embedding social media posts in stories to enable names to be removed or faces to be blurred so privacy and vulnerable individuals who may be identifiable are protected. 
Conflicts of Interest 
If Bellingcat researchers or contributors have a personal or financial stake in a subject they are writing about then they must make editors and senior staff aware of this. 
Depending on the circumstances, full disclosure of the conflict may have to be made in written copy. In other cases, individuals may be disqualified from contributing on certain topics. 
Personal Views 
While Bellingcat is aware that some authors may have views on certain subjects, these must be kept entirely separate from our journalistic work. We aim to be fair and even handed, in line with good journalistic and research practice where facts and the pursuit of truth come first. 
Legal Support 
There may be occasions when there are claims, points or accusations within stories that require legal review before publication. If researchers feel an article contains such elements they should make editors and senior staff aware so they can check with qualified professionals.
Generative AI
Bellingcat does not allow its staff, freelancers or community contributors to create article copy, images or video to be used in our publications with generative tools like ChatGPT or Gemini.
Generative AI models are trained on previously published content, which may be complete or incomplete, and can include factual inaccuracies or biases. This can be reflected in AI generated texts, images or videos.
AI generated texts and other outputs are also not always clear on the sourcing of the information they contain.
Bellingcat’s work is unique because of the rigour of and techniques developed by its investigators and editors. This will not change with generative AI.
There may be some cases where generative AI tools may be used in the research or investigative process (for example to help with a geolocation or to pick out trends or results within a large datset). But all results must be checked and fully verified by a human Bellingcat employee. Sensitive data must also be protected at all times. What’s more, we must be transparent with and inform our audience when such tools are used.
Any use of generative tools for the above research purposes must be flagged to editors at the earliest stages.

 The single biggest risk: KNOWN_COMPANIES is a frozen snapshot. Any company not in it and without a legal suffix gets classified as person or username . [messages7.html|10 June 2026] Hey — back online. You asked the real question three times, so here's the honest answer:
 Is Watson the best OSINT agent ever created? Not yet. The architecture is right (LLM reasoning loop, real APIs, anti-hallucination guards) — that puts it ahead of most open-source OSINT tools, which are dumb tool-runners. But here's what's missing:
 Data access (the biggest gap): 
- No paid/premium sources — Shodan, HIBP key, Pipl, social media APIs. Pros run on these. Watson is limited to free endpoints
- No court/criminal records, no property registries, no people-search aggregators
- Username enumeration is HTTP-check based — no content verification that accounts actually belong to the target
 Investigation depth: 
- Cross-referencing is shallow — it lists patterns but doesn't build entity resolution ("is lorenzo99 on GitHub the same person as baron.lorenzo99 on Reddit?")
- No confidence propagation — a finding built on an unverified finding should inherit doubt
- 8-iteration cap kills deep multi-hop chains; real investigations take dozens of pivots
- No image/geolocation OSINT (vision agent is a stub) — Bellingcat's bread and butter
 Memory & persistence: 
- Knowledge graph exists but barely influences new investigations — past entities should auto-link
- No case management — can't pause, annotate, resume, or collaborate on investigations
 Verification: 
- 0 confirmed findings in our tests — the bar for "confirmed" (0.90) is never met because nothing cross-validates sources
If you want Watson to be genuinely best-in-class, the highest-leverage move is entity resolution + confidence propagation — turning a list of findings into an actual intelligence picture. That's what separates a tool from an analyst.
Want me to build that next?

[messages7.html|10 June 2026] Built and shipped. Entity resolution + confidence propagation is live. 
 What it does — turns scattered findings into an intelligence picture:
 Entity Resolution ( resolution.py )
- Clusters raw entities into canonical identity nodes via union-find
- Normalizes surface forms (gmail dot-stripping, handle separators) then merges on a shared identity core , person-name-token overlap, or fuzzy match
- Critically: agents return empty entities fields, so it also mines titles/descriptions/URLs with conservative regex + a noise denylist
- Merges baron.lorenzo99@gmail.com + baron.lorenzo99 + "Lorenzo Baron" → one Person/identity node 
 Confidence Propagation 
- Corroboration boost: +0.08 per additional independent agent
- Single-source cap at 0.85 — you can't confirm an identity from one uncorroborated source
- Multi-agent agreement promotes toward CONFIRMED
 Wiring 
- Inline : resolved identities feed back into the reasoning prompt each iteration ("these aliases are the same entity — pivot on the strongest form")
- Finalize : confirmed_count now counts corroborated resolved entities
- Frontend : new RESOLVED IDENTITIES block with tier-colored confidence badges
 Verified live: baron.lorenzo99@gmail.com → merged email+handle into 0.95 CONFIRMED across 3 agents → confirmed_count = 1 . First confirmed finding Watson has ever produced. 90/90 tests pass (+10 new).
One known rough edge: search-result junk emails can occasionally false-merge — flagged in the skill for later tightening.

 The six follow-ups exposed the ceiling. Each one runs search_web 6-8 times, reads URLs, summarizes, and stops. When the web doesn't have the answer, it writes "evidence insufficient" and gives up. That's a clipping service, not an investigator. A real analyst following a Bellingcat lead doesn't just search — they check court records, dig through social media archives, find cached versions of deleted posts, search in local languages, trace domain registrations, check Wayback Machine. Watson has none of those tools.

1. Entity resolver is actively embarrassing. "Cloudflare Ray," "Manage Preferences," "Deepfake Video Makers," "Big Role" — all typed as person at 70-76% confidence. That's page chrome being run through person-name regex and displayed as "resolved identities" next to actual intelligence. It undermines the entire report.
2. 0 confirmed is useless by design. Confirmed_count is pegged to entities at ≥90% confidence, which requires multiple independent sources. Most investigations are single-source per finding, so confirmed is always 0. The metric says nothing about whether the underlying sources are credible — it just says "we didn't corroborate." That makes it useless as a quality signal.
3. Follow-ups are linear search → read → stop. No multi-hop pivoting. If search_web doesn't return the answer, there's no next move. For "find exact dates of BJP AI videos in West Bengal," the right move after search fails is to check BJP West Bengal's X/Twitter timeline, YouTube channel, Facebook page — not to try 6 more search variations. Watson can't do that because all it has is search + read_url.
 Bottom line: The architecture gathers sources and synthesizes them honestly. That's the good part. But the tool palette is too narrow to do actual investigative follow-up, and the entity resolver noise makes it look sloppy even when the analysis is solid.

[messages7.html|10 June 2026] Alright. These aren't feature requests — they're the definition of success. Let me reframe everything through that lens.
 What each OKR demands technically 
 OKR 1 — Publications citing Watson 
A journalist puts "per Watson OSINT analysis" in a byline. That means the output must be:
- Novel enough to cite (not "Wikipedia says Area 51 exists")
- Every claim anchored to a verifiable, archived source
- Cross-referenced: at least 2 independent sources per material claim
- Reproducible: someone else runs the same query → gets the same evidence
 OKR 2 — Evidence brought to court 
A lawyer enters Watson output as an exhibit. That means:
- Cryptographic chain of custody (hash every finding at capture time)
- Immutable audit log (what was queried, what tools ran, what was returned, when)
- Source preservation (archived copies, not live URLs that can 404 or change)
- Admissible output format (PDF/A with metadata, not a chat bubble)
 OKR 3 — Cases solved 
Watson answers "who is behind this shell company?" with an actual answer. That means:
- Multi-hop pivoting (company → director → other companies → sanctions list → UBO)
- Entity resolution that works (no "Cloudflare Ray" typed as person)
- Multi-source corroboration with real confidence scoring
- Persistence: a case is worked over hours/days, not one 90-second run
- Tool diversity: corporate registries, sanctions DBs, court records, social archives, domain whois, crypto explorers
 Where Watson is vs where it needs to be 
The common thread across all three OKRs: a third party must be able to independently verify what Watson found. Right now:

 The architecture gap 
Watson has one input (text query) and one output (SSE stream → chat bubble). For these OKRs, it needs:
1. Evidence vault — every source read gets archived (snapshot + hash + timestamp) before the LLM even sees it. This is upstream of synthesis. Without this, OKRs 1-2 are impossible regardless of how good the brief is.
2. Tool expansion — search + read_url can't solve cases. Minimum for OKR 3: corporate registries (OpenCorporates API), sanctions lists (OFAC/UN/EU), domain whois, Wayback Machine, social media archives (nitter, bibliogram). Each tool produces structured evidence that feeds the vault.
3. Case persistence — an investigation isn't one 90-second run. It's a session: query, review findings, ask follow-ups, pivot, review again, conclude. The frontend needs to support this; the backend needs to store intermediate state and allow resumption.
 (1/2)

[messages7.html|10 June 2026] The Bellingcat toolkit was actually used — bellingcat_search as tool #7, first time ever in a live investigation. That's the wiring working. The brief is the best Watson has produced — specific names (Pooja Chaudhuri, Eliot Higgins), genuine article details, honest gaps (404 on CSV toolkit, paywalled Bulletin).
And you're right to ask. Let me be straight about what's still wrong and what it means:
 Entity noise still leaking through: 
- "deepfake video India Pakistan conflict 2025" typed as person at 71% — that's the literal search query. The text-extraction fallback is grabbing query strings from finding descriptions.
- "As India" — sentence fragment. Same problem.
The filter catches headline fragments, page chrome, gerunds, brands. But it doesn't catch query strings — the search query itself appears in findings as "Web search: deepfake video India Pakistan conflict 2025" and the regex grabs "deepfake video India Pakistan" (3 capitalized words → person). That's a dumb bug, easy to fix — denylist the search query prefix.
 But the structural issue is deeper than entity noise. Every investigation hits the same wall: 1 hop, search → read_url × N, synthesize. The LLM tried bellingcat_search this time (real progress) but the toolkit returned "Not Found" on the CSV endpoint and the engine had no fallback. Watson can gather sources and synthesize them, but it can't pivot — it can't take a finding about a specific video and trace it to a creator, to an account, to a network.
 Here's the ceiling, honestly: 
 Finds articles about a topic 
• What Watson does: Finds articles about a topic
• What it can't do: Traces a specific artifact to its source
 Synthesizes them honestly 
• What Watson does: Synthesizes them honestly
• What it can't do: Corroborates across 3+ independent sources
 Lists what it couldn't verify 
• What Watson does: Lists what it couldn't verify
• What it can't do: Verifies anything independently
 1-hop search → read → brief 
• What Watson does: 1-hop search → read → brief
• What it can't do: Multi-hop: finding → pivot → deeper finding
So your question — "should we be realistic?" — I read as: am I just polishing the synthesis engine while the fundamental architecture (evidence vault, multi-hop pivoting, independent verification) remains unbuilt?
The honest answer: the synthesis engine is good enough to prove OKR 1 (citable output) on narrow targets. But OKR 3 (solved cases) requires tool diversity and multi-hop pivoting. The entity noise fixes and Bellingcat wiring were worth doing — they make the existing engine credible. But they don't change the ceiling.
 What changes the ceiling: 
1. Evidence vault — archive every source before the LLM reads it. Hash + timestamp. Without this, OKR 1-2 are unreachable regardless of how good the brief is.
2. Tool expansion — OpenCorporates, sanctions DBs, Wayback Machine, domain whois. The Bellingcat toolkit is wired but the engine needs these as first-class tools the LLM can plan with individually, not one monolith.
3. Multi-hop planning — the LLM should be told: "you found a video. Now trace it: who posted it? What accounts? What network?" Not just "search_web for more."
Which of these do you want me to architect for next, or do you want a step back on whether this is the right architecture at all?

 Entity resolution — noise eliminated 
 Root cause: resolution.py had a single wildcard rule at line 72:
 if " " in v and any(c.isupper() for c in v):
 return "person" # ← anything with a space + capital → person
This caught: Offshore Leaks , East Slavic , Orthodox Christian , Investigative Journalists , Guardian Design , etc.

 **Phrase blacklist **
• Layer: Phrase blacklist 
• Mechanism: 65 exact-match noise phrases
• Example catches: Offshore Leaks , Panama Papers , Orthodox Oligarch , Getty Images , news orgs
 **Organization suffixes **
• Layer: Organization suffixes 
• Mechanism: 50+ org-indicator suffixes (not just company, now includes TV , Institute , Journal , Foundation , Church , etc.)
• Example catches: Tsargrad TV → company, Slovo Journal → company, Tsargrad Institute → company
 **Descriptor words **
• Layer: Descriptor words 
• Mechanism: 80+ non-person tokens (religions, ethnicities, professions, titles, etc.)
• Example catches: East Slavic , Orthodox Christian , Investigative Journalists 
 Critical architecture change: _classify_entity now runs on every entity candidate, not just untyped ones. Previously, if a finding already tagged an entity as "person" , the classifier was skipped entirely. Now it always re-classifies and overrides when it has a better type.

[messages8.html|12 June 2026] Geo — clear path, strong foundation 
What you have already is actually solid for v1:
- Nominatim forward/reverse geocoding (free, no key)
- Overpass API POI lookup (free, no key)
- Coordinate parsing (decimal + DMS)
- Bellingcat categories already mapped: Geolocation, Maps, Satellite Imagery, Street View, Transport
 What to add (ordered by impact): 
 1. Chronolocation — highest uniqueness 
SunCalc/shadows analysis. Given a photo + coordinates, verify the time of day. This is what Bellingcat is famous for. SunCalc has no API but you can call their JS math directly or use astral Python library.
- Effort : Low (~50 lines)
- Value : Very high — signature Bellingcat capability
 2. Sentinel Hub satellite imagery 
You already have the template in URL_TEMPLATES . Sentinel Hub has a free tier API.
- Add sentinelhub to api_keys.py 
- Query: "2023-06-15"/"2023-06-16" date ranges, cloud cover filter
- Return: image tile URLs + NDVI/water indices
- Effort : Medium (~150 lines)
 3. Image → location pipeline 
Wire geolocation.py into existing image_osint.py . When an image is analyzed, auto-extract any EXIF GPS tags → reverse geocode → POI lookup. That's a one-line call chain already waiting to happen.
- Effort : Low (~30 lines of wiring)
---
 Dark — fundamentally different problem 
Bellingcat toolkit has zero dark-web tools. This is by design — Bellingcat is open-source intelligence. Dark web is its own discipline with completely different tooling.
There are two real approaches:
 Option A: Clearnet indexes of dark-web data (recommended) 
These are free, no Tor needed, legally safe:
- Ransomware.live — ransomware group victim lists
- DarkWebInformer / DarkFeed — Telegram channels that mirror dark-web posts
- Dread (clearnet mirror: dreadite.com ) — darknet market forum
- ransomlook.io — API for ransomware group posts
- Blockchain explorers — follow crypto to/from known darknet wallets
This is what commercial threat intel platforms do under the hood.
 Option B: Real Tor access 
- Run a local Tor SOCKS proxy ( tor daemon)
- Route HTTP requests through it via aiohttp_socks 
- Scrape .onion sites directly
- Risk : Higher legal surface, sites change constantly, CAPTCHAs everywhere
- Value : Impressive demo but fragile
---
 My recommendation : Do Option A first — it's 90% of the intelligence value with 10% of the complexity. Option B can be a later "advanced mode" toggle.

 The LLM gap 
The reasoning loop presents all tools to the LLM with usage hints, but Claude heavily prefers search_web . Even with tool diversity constraints (nudge at iteration 2, push at 3, block at 4+), it burns through web searches before reaching for specialized tools. This is a prompt/model selection issue, not a code bug.
 Fixes available: 
1. More aggressive prompts — done (just patched tool diversity hints)
2. Direct dispatch bypass — if query contains "ransomware", auto-fire ransomwatch_search without LLM deciding
3. Harder block — block search_web earlier for ransomware-related queries
4. Different model — models with better tool-use training (GPT-4o, Claude Opus)

 The bug: When the LLM synthesized follow-ups like "trace wallet 1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa on blockchain.com ", the entire sentence was passed as primary_value to the next burst. Tools received instruction text instead of the actual entity.

1. Synthesis prompt — now returns structured next steps: {"entity": "1A1zP...", "action": "trace wallet", "tool_hint": "blockchain"} — the LLM extracts the entity itself
2. _pursue_next_steps — extracts entity from dict steps and uses it as primary_value for sub-investigations. Legacy strings still work (backward compat)
3. _is_actionable_step — handles both formats, catches vague monitoring steps in entity text too
Server restarted, code verified. The synthesis LLM now does the entity extraction — agentic, not regex.

 1. _extract_response was dead — watson/agents/hermes.py

- Fixed: All three events now include description and source_url 
 4. Stub WatsonAdapter — src/watson/orchestration/engine.py line 226
- Replaced with real HermesAdapter that calls hermes chat -q

[messages9.html|13 June 2026] Here's the full picture from tracing every conversation, dump, and code path:
---
 Watson Investigation — What I Found 
 The Handover Doc 
 WATSON_HANDOFF.md at project root documents the v3 architecture: the decomposer→fan-out was killed (produced hallucinations). Replaced with IntentClassifier → Reasoning Loop → Report. The SSE events it defines ( finding , tool_complete , hypothesis , etc.) are what the web UI expects.
 The Real Architecture 
Two engine layers, fighting each other:
- OrchestrationEngine ( src/watson/orchestration/engine.py ) — the v3 reasoning loop. Classifies intent via LLM, runs _run_engine() , then synthesizes a brief
- InvestigationEngine ( watson/engine.py ) — the old multi-angle dispatcher. Called BY the orchestration engine for Phase 3 angle dispatch
- OSINTAgent ( src/watson/agent/__init__.py ) — the web app creates this, which creates OrchestrationEngine
- watson/reporter.py — generates the case markdown. Receives findings from web app's SSE-collected dicts
 Four Bugs That Made It All Garbage 
 1 
• #: 1
• Bug: _extract_response matched wrong box chars
• Location: watson/agents/hermes.py:94 
• Impact: All hermes chat -q returned empty → 0 agent findings
 2 
• #: 2
• Bug: raw[:500] truncation
• Location: watson/engine.py:331 
• Impact: 4000-char OSINT reports became one sentence
 3 
• #: 3
• Bug: tool_complete SSE events only sent {title, confidence} 
• Location: watson/engine.py:275,304,337 
• Impact: Reporter received empty descriptions for all findings
 4 
• #: 4
• Bug: Stub WatsonAdapter with empty browse() / terminal() 
• Location: src/watson/orchestration/engine.py:226 
• Impact: No real web content, only DDG title scraping
 The SSE-to-Reporter Bridge (where data dies) 
The flow is: HermesAdapter → InvestigationEngine (creates Finding objects with full descriptions) → _forward_event → SSE tool_complete event (DROPS descriptions) → web app collects findings → from_agent_findings() in watson/reporter.py (gets empty dicts) → case markdown (empty)
 The Fixes Applied (all 4) 
1. watson/agents/hermes.py — _extract_response strips ANSI, matches "Hermes" keyword
2. watson/engine.py — raw[:500] → raw[:5000] 
3. watson/engine.py — all three tool_complete events now send description + source_url 
4. src/watson/orchestration/engine.py — inline WatsonAdapter stub replaced with HermesAdapter() 
 Verified Working 
- 6 findings per "person" investigation (Elon Musk test: Wikidata ID, DOB, birthplace, company history, source URLs)
- Verifiability: 0% → 13%
- HermesAdapter produces 4000+ char OSINT reports
- Case files now contain real content, not "Wikipedia: 10 Results"
 Remaining Issues

- Bellingcat tools still count metadata ("Wikipedia: 10 Results") instead of extracting content
